selection.description: Curated starter selection of ten verified Astrid S recordings spanning solo singles, two named collaborations, EP material, and the Joyride era. The listed order is editorial presentation order, not a chart rank.
limitations: Spotify artist Top tracks were encountered, but cached/retrieved renderings did not yield a consistent current top ten or stable market; no Spotify Popular ranking is claimed.
Spotify track embed URLs establish recorded artist credits but do not independently prove availability in every market.
Release dates describe the named verified edition and need not equal earliest live performance or first issue.

artist.name: Astrid S
artist.short_description: Norwegian pop singer-songwriter whose catalogue pairs relationship-focused writing with polished pop and electronic influences.
artist.biography: Astrid S is the recording name of Astrid Smeplass, a Norwegian singer and songwriter from Berkåk in the Rennebu area. She received piano and singing tuition while growing up, and also learned flute and guitar. Her wider public breakthrough came after finishing fifth on Norway’s Idol in 2013; she subsequently signed with Universal Music. The self-titled Astrid S EP arrived in 2016 and included Hurts So Good, which became one of her signature releases. Party’s Over followed in 2017, a period that also brought Breathe, Such A Boy and Think Before I Talk. She earned a Norwegian Spellemann newcomer prize for 2016 and the Artist of the Year honor for 2017. Her debut studio album, Leave It Beautiful, appeared in October 2020. Her official biography frames the album as personal writing shaped by breakups, major changes and the experience of growing up; It’s Ok If You Forget Me is one of its key songs. Her second studio album, Joyride, followed in May 2024. In a contemporary interview, she compared the title track’s fleeting romance with her approach to enjoying life without dwelling on uncertain outcomes. Across these releases, her documented pop background sits alongside electronic and R&B influences, while the emotional range stretches from argument and regret to infatuation and acceptance. For Afterglow, the attraction is the contrast between accessible pop songwriting and emotionally complicated stories; that final characterization is editorial, not an official genre designation.

Her self-titled EP was released in 2016 and Party’s Over in 2017.

songs.title: Hurts So Good
songs.release_date_context: Verified on the 2016 self-titled EP; precise original standalone-single issue date is not independently established.
songs.short_description: A signature Astrid S recording about wanting a relationship that also causes pain.
songs.editorial_notes: Start here for a relationship story built around attraction and incompatibility. This framing follows the artist’s own interview, not independent audio listening.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid described a couple strongly drawn to one another even though being together is painful or impossible, and said she related to the song although she did not write it.

related_songs.explanation: Moves from painful attraction to damage caused by conflict.
Follows the aftermath of a relationship that no longer works.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify identifies this recording as Hurts So Good by Astrid S.
A version was on her 2016 self-titled EP.
Astrid explained the song’s painful attraction and distinguished herself from its writers.

uncertainties: Exact first-release day is not confirmed here; do not treat the 2021 remix or reissue as the original.

songs.title: Think Before I Talk
songs.release_date_context: 2017 standalone single, before later compilation or complete-album appearances.
songs.short_description: A pop single addressing words spoken in anger and the regret that follows.
songs.editorial_notes: Use for a playlist about conversations people wish they could undo; the subject is described in the release announcement and in Astrid’s interviews.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid said it concerns hurtful things people say when angry or frustrated. In a separate interview, she clarified that she did not write the song, though she identifies with its message.

related_songs.explanation: Both examine hurt within a relationship.
Both revisit emotional consequences after a relationship changes.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify confirms this single recording and Astrid S credit.
The standalone single was released August 25 2017.
Astrid spoke about conflict and explicitly said she was not the song’s writer.

songs.title: It's Ok If You Forget Me
songs.release_date_context: Originally reported as a single on this date, ahead of its appearance on Leave It Beautiful in October 2020.
songs.release_title: It's Ok If You Forget Me
songs.short_description: A breakup song reflecting on the unsettling absence, or delay, of expected heartbreak.
songs.editorial_notes: A useful Afterglow entry for songs where the narrator seems unexpectedly composed after a split. Independent reviews support that reading; it is not inferred from the title alone.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: In a 2023 Q&A transcript, Astrid reportedly explained that the song was written about an ex and that its apparent reassurance partly masked her struggle to cope. This paraphrase should be verified against the original recording before publishing as a definitive quote of intent.

related_songs.explanation: A contrasting way of handling feelings after a breakup.
An emotional sequel to a difficult attachment.

supported_claims.claim: Official Spotify embed identifies the selected track and performer.
Contemporary reporting establishes the September 18 2020 single and subsequent album release.
The 2023 interview transcript records Astrid’s comments, though transcription quality remains unverified.

uncertainties: 2023 commentary comes from an automatically generated Norwegian podcast transcript; confirm against audio before attributing strongly.

songs.title: I Do
songs.release_date_context: Original collaborative single, separate from later Leave It Beautiful (Complete) placement.
songs.short_description: A duet about admitting that feelings for a former partner remain.
songs.editorial_notes: The two credited vocalists give Afterglow an example of a pop-country crossover, while contemporary reporting grounds the lingering-feelings theme. No independent audio analysis was performed.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid said country music had influenced her songwriting and welcomed Brett Young on the song; Young emphasized the story and lyrics when discussing why he joined. Neither statement is treated as a detailed autobiographical account.

related_songs.explanation: Both consider what remains emotionally after a breakup.
Both center on unresolved romantic attachment.

supported_claims.claim: Official Spotify embed names Astrid S and Brett Young.
Apple Music lists the original duet single on February 28 2020.
Contemporaneous trade reporting quotes both artists on influences and song storytelling.

songs.title: Favorite Part Of Me
songs.release_date_context: Documented on Down Low in late September 2019; Apple lists September 26 while a Norwegian label announcement dated September 26 said the EP would arrive at midnight. This is an EP-edition date, not a verified earliest public performance.
songs.short_description: A personal song of gratitude for people who help someone become their best self.
songs.editorial_notes: Rather than assuming a romantic dedication, frame it around positive influence from close relationships: the artist specifically mentioned friends and family.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid explained that different people affect her differently, and she wrote this song to celebrate friends and family who draw out the best version of herself.

related_songs.explanation: Moves from gratitude toward moments of overwhelming affection.
Both feature self-awareness in relationships, though with different tones.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify confirms the recording is credited to Astrid S.
Late-September 2019 Down Low EP inclusion is confirmed by label announcement and Apple Music.
Astrid explained the personal inspiration in an interview.

uncertainties: Day-level EP release differs by retailer/time-zone framing; month precision is deliberate.
Earlier live performances are documented, so the EP date should not be characterized as the first time the song was heard.

songs.title: Breathe
songs.release_date_context: Original single issued in March 2017, subsequently included on Party’s Over in June 2017.
songs.short_description: A pop song about the breathless feeling of falling hard for a person or an extraordinary moment.
songs.editorial_notes: Use for playlists about the intensity of a new feeling; the artist distinguished the emotion from being about any one specific partner.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid said the song captures being swept away and losing one’s breath; for her, it also represented exciting moments from the preceding year rather than a single love interest.

related_songs.explanation: Both express positive emotion brought out by others.
Both can fit a brighter relationship-focused collection.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify embed confirms this Astrid S track.
Contemporaneous interview dates the release to March 10 2017.
Astrid gave the song-specific explanation in a March 2017 interview.

songs.title: Such A Boy
songs.release_date_context: Verified Party’s Over EP edition date; a separate earlier single-premiere date was not established.
songs.short_description: A sharp pop song that questions gendered expectations and uncertain behavior while dating.
songs.editorial_notes: More pointed and playful than the breakup-oriented entries here; this description draws from the artist’s discussion of how the song was written, not from a claimed listening session.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid described writing it with Cass Lowe around confusion in dating and the unfair use of gendered insults that frame girls as overly emotional.

related_songs.explanation: Both explore how language affects relationships.
Both use more assertive, playful relationship framing.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify embed identifies Such A Boy by Astrid S.
Apple Music dates the Party’s Over EP to June 30 2017.
Astrid discussed the song’s social and dating themes in an interview.

uncertainties: The date is for the documented EP edition, not a independently verified first standalone release.

songs.title: I Don't Know Why
songs.release_date_context: Collaborative single credited to NOTD and Astrid S, not an Astrid-only solo original.
songs.short_description: An electronic-pop collaboration joining NOTD’s production with Astrid S’s vocals.
songs.editorial_notes: The original Q&A explains how the collaboration and vocal recording came together. It is a useful stylistic detour within the selection, but there is insufficient song-specific first-person evidence here to assert the intended lyrical story.
songs.editorial_notes_basis: NOTD interview and catalog credits; no direct listening

related_songs.explanation: Shows another contemporary pop setting for Astrid’s vocals.
Offers another brighter selection alongside relationship-focused pop.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify embed names NOTD first and Astrid S second.
Apple Music dates the original single May 8 2020 and credits both acts.
Interview with NOTD confirms collaboration workflow but does not establish intended lyrical meaning.

uncertainties: No sufficiently explicit Astrid S song-meaning statement was verified; leave the artist-statement field null.

songs.title: Two Hands
songs.release_date_context: Original single, later included on the May 2024 Joyride album.
songs.short_description: A playful relationship song presenting both attractive traits and personal complications.
songs.editorial_notes: An editorial bridge from Such A Boy: both approach dating with humor or provocation instead of straightforward sadness. The label announcement, not unverified audio playback, is the basis for this framing.
songs.editorial_notes_basis: official label release and artist statement
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid characterized the song as a note to future partners: she has good and difficult sides, but believes the experience together can still be enjoyable.

related_songs.explanation: Both present an assertive, less melancholy side of relationship pop.
Both belong to the Joyride period and embrace imperfect experiences.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify embed confirms Astrid S recording.
Apple Music and label announce January 12 2024 as the single release date.
Official Universal Music Norge announcement includes Astrid’s direct song-specific explanation.

songs.title: Joyride
songs.release_date_context: Title track from second studio album of the same name, dated May 24 2024.
songs.short_description: An album title track using a temporary romance as a metaphor for enjoying uncertain experiences.
songs.editorial_notes: A fitting closer for the starter selection: the artist’s own comparison broadens the song from romance to an outlook on creative life. This is interview-based analysis, not a claimed audio review.
songs.artist_statement_paraphrase: Astrid described the track as entering a relationship one suspects will not last while choosing to enjoy it, and related that idea to not worrying prematurely about her career.

related_songs.explanation: Both represent the 2024 Joyride era and acknowledge imperfect romance.
Contrasts post-breakup reflection with willingness to enjoy something uncertain.

supported_claims.claim: Spotify embed confirms recording and artist.
Apple Music dates Joyride to May 24 2024.
Astrid explained the relationship-as-journey metaphor in an original 2024 interview.
